title: The ACMG/AMP variant classification framework
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015;17:405
text: The 2015 joint recommendation of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Association for Molecular Pathology sorts germline sequence variants in Mendelian disease genes into five classes: pathogenic, likely pathogenic, uncertain significance, likely benign and benign. Evidence is organised into 28 criteria, each with a direction (pathogenic or benign) and a default strength: very strong, strong, moderate or supporting for pathogenic evidence, and stand alone, strong or supporting for benign evidence. Criteria fall into population, computational, functional, segregation, de novo, allelic, database and other evidence types. Likely pathogenic and likely benign were intended to mean at least 90% certainty. The framework applies to a variant and a specific disease, assumes the gene disease relationship is established, and does not cover somatic, copy number or pharmacogenomic variants.

title: PVS1: null variant in a loss of function gene
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
Abou Tayoun AN et al. Hum Mutat 2018;39:1517
text: PVS1 applies to predicted null variants (nonsense, frameshift, canonical plus or minus one and two splice sites, initiation codon, single or multiexon deletion) in a gene where loss of function is an established disease mechanism. The ClinGen SVI decision tree refines it: a premature stop predicted to trigger nonsense mediated decay keeps very strong; a stop that escapes decay is downgraded to strong when the removed region is critical or removes more than about ten percent of the protein, and to moderate otherwise; canonical splice variants are graded by whether skipping the exon disrupts the reading frame and how much protein is removed; initiation codon variants are usually moderate. PVS1 should not be applied when loss of function is not the mechanism, for example in genes where disease arises from gain of function.

title: Nonsense mediated decay and the 50 nucleotide rule
refs: Abou Tayoun AN et al. Hum Mutat 2018
Nagy E, Maquat LE. Trends Biochem Sci 1998
text: Transcripts with a premature termination codon are usually degraded by nonsense mediated decay, which removes the protein product entirely. Decay is expected when the premature stop lies more than about 50 to 55 nucleotides upstream of the last exon junction complex. A premature stop in the last exon, or within the last 50 nucleotides of the penultimate exon, is predicted to escape decay and to produce a truncated protein. For frameshift variants the relevant position is the new stop codon created downstream, not the first altered residue. Single exon genes and genes with alternative transcripts need care, because decay prediction depends on the exon structure of the transcript that is expressed in the relevant tissue.

title: Canonical splice site variants and exon skipping
refs: Abou Tayoun AN et al. Hum Mutat 2018
Walker LC et al. Am J Hum Genet 2023;110:1046
text: Changes at the invariant plus or minus one and two positions of an intron are predicted to abolish the splice donor or acceptor. The most common outcome is skipping of the adjacent exon; cryptic splice site use and intron retention also occur. If skipping removes a number of coding bases that is not a multiple of three, the reading frame shifts and the variant behaves like a frameshift, so PVS1 can stay very strong when decay is expected. If skipping keeps the frame, the strength depends on whether the removed exon encodes a critical region or a substantial share of the protein. RNA studies showing the actual splicing outcome are the best evidence and can replace the prediction.

title: Initiation codon variants
refs: Abou Tayoun AN et al. Hum Mutat 2018
text: A change that destroys the ATG initiation codon may prevent translation, but ribosomes can often start at the next in frame methionine and produce an N terminally truncated protein. The SVI decision tree therefore applies PVS1 at moderate strength to initiation codon variants by default, raising it only if there are no alternative start codons nearby and pathogenic variants are known upstream of the closest alternative start, which shows that the skipped region matters.

title: PS1: same amino acid change as an established pathogenic variant
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
Walker LC et al. Am J Hum Genet 2023
text: PS1 applies when a different nucleotide change produces the same amino acid change as a variant already established as pathogenic, for example c.35G>A and c.35G>C both giving p.Gly12Asp. The curator must check that the established variant acts through the protein change rather than through splicing. The ClinGen SVI splicing group extended the idea to splicing: a variant at the same splice position as a pathogenic splicing variant, with a similar predicted effect, may receive PS1 at a strength that depends on the location and on how well the comparison variant's splicing effect is established.

title: PS2 and PM6: de novo occurrence
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
ClinGen SVI recommendation for de novo criteria (2018, version 1.1)
text: A variant that arose de novo in a patient with the disease and no family history is evidence for pathogenicity because new mutations in any given gene are rare. PS2 requires confirmed maternity and paternity; PM6 covers assumed de novo occurrence without confirmed parentage. The SVI points scale weights each observation: a confirmed de novo variant in a patient with a phenotype highly specific for the gene scores two points and one with a consistent but non specific phenotype one point, while assumed de novo observations score half as much. Summed points map to supporting (0.5), moderate (1), strong (2) and very strong (4). The phenotype must fit the gene's disease.

title: PS3 and BS3: functional studies
refs: Brnich SE et al. Genome Med 2020;12:3
text: Well established functional assays showing a damaging effect support pathogenicity (PS3); showing no effect supports a benign interpretation (BS3). The ClinGen SVI recommendation asks four questions: what the disease mechanism is, which classes of assay reflect it, whether the specific assay is validated with enough pathogenic and benign controls, and how the result applies to the variant. The strength is derived from the assay's OddsPath, computed from control variants: with at least eleven controls of known class an assay can reach strong evidence, with fewer it is limited to moderate or supporting. Results from patient cells, animal models and splicing assays each have particular caveats.

title: PS4: prevalence in affected individuals
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: PS4 applies when a variant is significantly more common in affected individuals than in controls, classically with an odds ratio above five and a confidence interval that excludes one. For rare variants, where case control studies lack power, many expert panels instead count unrelated affected probands carrying the variant, with thresholds such as two, four or more probands for supporting, moderate or strong, provided the variant is absent or very rare in population databases. Counting the same proband twice, for example through overlapping publications and ClinVar submissions, is a common error.

title: PM1: mutational hot spot or critical domain
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: PM1 applies to missense variants located in a mutational hot spot or in a well studied functional domain where many pathogenic variants cluster and benign variation is absent. Expert panels usually define the qualifying residues or regions explicitly, for example the activating hot spots of RAS pathway genes. A data driven version counts pathogenic and benign missense variants in a window around the residue. Because computational predictors often already capture regional constraint, ClinGen advises that PM1 and PP3 together should not exceed strong evidence.

title: PM2: absent or extremely rare in population databases
refs: ClinGen SVI recommendation for absence or rarity (PM2), version 1.0, 2020
Karczewski KJ et al. Nature 2020;581:434
text: A variant that is absent from large population databases such as gnomAD, or extremely rare for a recessive disorder, is more likely to be pathogenic. The SVI working group recommended in 2020 that PM2 be applied at supporting strength by default, because absence alone is weak evidence: most rare variants in the population are benign and simply unobserved. The curator should confirm that the region is adequately covered by sequencing in the database, since a variant can be absent because the site is poorly captured. For recessive disorders a low frequency compatible with carrier status can still qualify.

title: PM3: detected in trans with a pathogenic variant
refs: ClinGen SVI recommendation for in trans criterion (PM3), version 1.0
text: For recessive disorders, finding the variant in trans with a pathogenic variant in affected individuals supports pathogenicity. The SVI points scale gives one point per proband when the other allele is pathogenic and phase is confirmed in trans, half a point when the other allele is likely pathogenic or phase is unknown, and half a point for homozygous occurrence (counted only once). Points map to supporting (0.5), moderate (1), strong (2) and very strong (4). Observations must be in unrelated probands with a phenotype consistent with the disease.

title: PM4: protein length change
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: In frame deletions or insertions and stop loss variants change protein length and support pathogenicity at moderate strength when they fall outside repetitive regions. Expert panels often reduce PM4 to supporting for the deletion or insertion of a single residue, and PM4 is not combined with PVS1 for the same effect. In frame changes in repetitive or poorly conserved regions without known function point the other way and are captured by BP3.

title: PM5: different pathogenic missense change at the same residue
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: PM5 applies to a novel missense change at an amino acid residue where a different missense change is already established as pathogenic, on the reasoning that the residue is functionally important. The new substitution should be at least as damaging biochemically as the established one. Some expert panels raise PM5 to strong when two or more different pathogenic changes are known at the residue, and downgrade it when the established variant is only likely pathogenic. PM5 is not combined with PS1 for the same residue.

title: PP1 and BS4: segregation with disease
refs: Jarvik GP, Browning BL. Am J Hum Genet 2016;98:1077
text: Cosegregation of a variant with disease in a family provides evidence proportional to the number of informative meioses. Under a dominant model each informative meiosis halves the chance of cosegregation by chance, so three meioses give odds of about 8 to 1 (supporting), five about 32 to 1 (moderate) and seven about 128 to 1 (strong). Jarvik and Browning recommend counting meioses across families and not upgrading beyond what the counts justify. Lack of segregation in affected relatives (BS4) is strong benign evidence, but phenocopies, reduced penetrance and late onset must be considered.

title: PP2 and BP1: gene level missense evidence
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: PP2 supports pathogenicity for a missense variant in a gene with a low rate of benign missense variation where missense variants are a common cause of disease. BP1 points the other way for a missense variant in a gene where disease is caused mainly by truncating variants, as in many tumour suppressor genes. Both are gene level, supporting evidence and can be derived from the spectrum of classified variants in the gene, ideally excluding the variant under review. Some expert panels decline to use PP2 because modern missense predictors already encode gene level constraint.

title: PP3 and BP4: computational evidence
refs: Pejaver V et al. Am J Hum Genet 2022;109:2163
text: Computational predictions support pathogenicity (PP3) or a benign interpretation (BP4). The original guideline asked curators to require agreement among several tools, which mixes correlated predictors. In 2022 the ClinGen SVI working group calibrated individual tools so that score intervals map to evidence strengths: with a prior probability of 0.0441 the positive likelihood ratio needed is about 2.4 for supporting, 5.8 for moderate, 33.5 for strong and 1124 for very strong. Several missense tools reach strong for PP3 and moderate or strong for BP4 in their extreme ranges. A single calibrated tool should be chosen in advance and used consistently.

title: PP4: phenotype specificity
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: PP4 applies when the patient's phenotype or family history is highly specific for a disease with a single genetic cause, so that finding a variant in that gene is itself informative. It is supporting evidence and should not be used for common or genetically heterogeneous phenotypes. A structured approach compares the patient's Human Phenotype Ontology terms with the disease profile of the gene and asks how unusual the match is compared with random genes; a strong match to a distinctive profile justifies PP4, a generic match does not.

title: PP5 and BP6 retired
refs: Biesecker LG, Harrison SM. Genet Med 2018;20:1687
text: PP5 and BP6 allowed a reputable source's classification to count as evidence without sharing the underlying data. The ClinGen SVI working group recommended in 2018 that both criteria no longer be used, because they risk counting the same evidence twice and reward assertions rather than data. Curators should instead evaluate the evidence that the reputable source relied on. Allelion Verdict AI never uses a variant's own ClinVar assertion as evidence.

title: BA1: stand alone benign frequency
refs: Ghosh R et al. Genet Med 2018;20:1235
text: A variant whose allele frequency exceeds five percent in any general continental population with adequate sample size is classified benign on that evidence alone. The ClinGen SVI working group clarified that the frequency should come from a population with at least 2000 observed alleles, and published a short exception list of well known common variants that are pathogenic or act as risk alleles despite high frequency, such as the HFE p.Cys282Tyr and p.His63Asp variants and GJB2 p.Val37Ile. Genes with high frequency founder alleles need gene specific thresholds.

title: BS1: frequency greater than expected for the disorder
refs: Whiffin N et al. Genet Med 2017;19:1151
text: BS1 applies when the variant is more common in the population than the disorder can explain. Whiffin and colleagues formalised this as the maximum credible population allele frequency: for a dominant disorder, prevalence times the largest share of cases attributable to a single variant (allelic contribution), divided by penetrance; for a recessive disorder, the square root of prevalence times the allelic contribution. A variant whose filtering allele frequency (the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval in the population with the highest frequency) exceeds the maximum credible frequency is too common to be a highly penetrant cause.

title: BS2: observed in healthy individuals
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: BS2 applies when a variant is observed in healthy adults in a state that should cause disease: homozygous for a fully penetrant recessive disorder, hemizygous for an X linked disorder, or heterozygous for a fully penetrant dominant disorder with early onset. Population databases such as gnomAD exclude individuals with severe paediatric disease, but they do include people with adult onset or mild conditions, so BS2 is unreliable for late onset disorders and genes with reduced penetrance.

title: BP2: observed with another pathogenic variant
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: BP2 supports a benign interpretation when the variant is observed in trans with a pathogenic variant in a gene for a fully penetrant dominant disorder, because two damaging alleles would usually cause a more severe or different phenotype, or in cis with a pathogenic variant in any gene, because the pathogenic variant already explains the disease. Phase must be established for the in trans case.

title: BP3: in frame change in a repetitive region
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: BP3 applies to in frame deletions or insertions in a repetitive region without a known function, such as polyglutamine or polyalanine tracts that tolerate length variation. Evidence that the region tolerates variation can come from benign in frame variants nearby or from low conservation. BP3 and PM4 are mutually exclusive.

title: BP5: alternate molecular basis for disease
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: BP5 applies when the variant is found in a case that has another molecular cause for the disease. Its value is limited in disorders where multiple variants can contribute, such as inherited cancer predisposition, and in conditions with digenic or oligogenic inheritance.

title: BP7: synonymous and intronic variants without splice impact
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
Walker LC et al. Am J Hum Genet 2023
text: BP7 applies to synonymous variants for which splice prediction shows no impact and the nucleotide is not highly conserved. The ClinGen SVI splicing group extended BP7 to intronic variants at or beyond position plus seven on the donor side and minus twenty one on the acceptor side, when no splice impact is predicted. Synonymous changes in the last three bases or the first base of an exon sit in the exonic part of the splice consensus and should not receive BP7 without a confident prediction of no effect.

title: The Bayesian point system
refs: Tavtigian SV et al. Genet Med 2018;20:1054
Tavtigian SV et al. Hum Mutat 2020;41:1734
text: Tavtigian and colleagues showed that the ACMG/AMP combining rules behave like a naive Bayesian classifier in which evidence strengths are powers of one odds unit: supporting, moderate, strong and very strong correspond to odds of pathogenicity of 350 raised to the powers one eighth, one quarter, one half and one. Converting to points (supporting 1, moderate 2, strong 4, very strong 8, with benign criteria negative) lets evidence be summed, including conflicting evidence. A total of ten or more points is pathogenic, six to nine likely pathogenic, zero to five uncertain, minus one to minus six likely benign and minus seven or fewer benign.

title: Posterior probability of pathogenicity
refs: Tavtigian SV et al. Genet Med 2018
text: Under the Bayesian adaptation the posterior probability of pathogenicity is the prior times the combined odds, normalised: posterior equals odds times prior divided by odds minus one times prior plus one, with a prior of 0.10 and combined odds of 350 raised to points divided by eight. Likely pathogenic corresponds to a posterior between 0.90 and 0.99 and pathogenic to above 0.99, matching the intent of the 2015 guideline that likely means at least ninety percent certainty.

title: The original 2015 combining rules
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: The 2015 guideline lists explicit combinations. Pathogenic requires one very strong with at least one strong, two moderate, one moderate and one supporting, or two supporting; or two or more strong; or one strong with three moderate, two moderate and two supporting, or one moderate and four supporting. Likely pathogenic requires one very strong with one moderate, one strong with one or two moderate, one strong with two supporting, three moderate, two moderate with two supporting, or one moderate with four supporting. Benign requires one stand alone or two strong; likely benign requires one strong and one supporting or two supporting. When pathogenic and benign evidence conflict the variant is uncertain.

title: Filtering allele frequency and population maximum
refs: Karczewski KJ et al. Nature 2020
Whiffin N et al. Genet Med 2017
text: Population frequency should be judged in the genetic ancestry group where the variant is most common, because many variants are population specific. The filtering allele frequency is the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval of the allele frequency in that group; using it protects against chance enrichment in small samples. Founder variants can be common in one population and rare elsewhere, so a single global frequency can hide relevant structure. Bottlenecked populations such as Ashkenazi Jewish and Finnish groups are usually excluded from the filtering calculation.

title: Gene disease validity
refs: Strande NT et al. Am J Hum Genet 2017;100:895
text: Variant classification assumes that the gene is truly associated with the disease. The ClinGen gene disease validity framework grades the relationship as definitive, strong, moderate, limited, disputed or refuted using genetic and experimental evidence. Classifying variants as pathogenic in a gene with limited or disputed evidence is not appropriate; such variants should usually remain of uncertain significance until the gene disease relationship is established.

title: Variants of uncertain significance
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: A variant of uncertain significance should not be used for clinical decision making, including predictive testing of relatives. Uncertain variants are common, especially missense variants in large genes, and most are eventually reclassified as benign or likely benign when more data accumulate. Laboratories periodically reassess them as population data, functional assays and case reports grow, and some report a sub tier (leaning pathogenic or leaning benign) internally to prioritise review.

title: ClinVar review status and conflicting interpretations
refs: Landrum MJ et al. Nucleic Acids Res 2018
text: ClinVar aggregates submitted interpretations and summarises their review status with stars: no assertion criteria (zero stars), criteria provided by a single submitter (one star), multiple submitters with no conflicts (two stars), reviewed by an expert panel (three stars) and practice guideline (four stars). Conflicting interpretations arise when submitters disagree, often between uncertain and likely benign. Expert panel classifications follow gene specific rules and are the closest public reference standard, which is why Allelion Verdict AI uses them as its blind test set.

title: HGVS nomenclature basics
refs: den Dunnen JT et al. Hum Mutat 2016;37:564
text: HGVS describes variants relative to a reference sequence. Coding positions (c.) count from the A of the ATG start codon as c.1; the base before it is c.-1 and the 5 prime untranslated region is negative, while the 3 prime untranslated region is numbered from the stop codon with an asterisk (c.*1). Intronic bases are given as the nearest exonic base plus or minus an offset, so c.375+1G>A is the first base of the intron after c.375. Substitutions use >, deletions del, duplications dup, insertions ins and combined changes delins. Protein changes (p.) use three letter amino acid codes, Ter or * for stop, fs for frameshift and = for synonymous; predicted consequences should be written in parentheses.

title: Choice of reference transcript
refs: Morales J et al. Nature 2022;604:310
text: The same genomic variant can have different c. and p. descriptions on different transcripts, and an exon can be coding in one transcript and untranslated or absent in another. The Matched Annotation from NCBI and EMBL EBI (MANE) project defines one agreed transcript per gene for reporting. Decay predictions, exon numbering and in frame skipping all depend on the transcript, so the transcript used for PVS1 decisions should be the clinically relevant one, and alternative transcripts expressed in the disease tissue should be considered.

title: Expert panel specifications
refs: Rivera Munoz EA et al. Hum Mutat 2018;39:1614
text: ClinGen variant curation expert panels adapt the general criteria to individual genes and diseases: they set gene specific frequency thresholds for BA1, BS1 and PM2, define hot spots and critical domains for PM1, choose a calibrated predictor and its thresholds for PP3 and BP4, decide which functional assays qualify for PS3, and sometimes disable criteria such as PP2. Their specifications are published in the ClinGen criteria specification registry and their classifications are deposited in ClinVar with three star review status.

title: BRCA1 and BRCA2 classification by ENIGMA
refs: Spurdle AB et al. Hum Mutat 2012;33:2
Parsons MT et al. Hum Mutat 2019;40:1557
text: The ENIGMA consortium classifies BRCA1 and BRCA2 variants using multifactorial likelihood models that combine prior probability from bioinformatic prediction, cosegregation, co occurrence with a pathogenic variant, family history and tumour pathology. Truncating variants upstream of the known functional limits are classified pathogenic; specific rules govern variants that escape decay near the 3 prime end, and splicing effects are weighed with RNA studies. ENIGMA classifications dominate the expert panel records for these genes in ClinVar.

title: Mismatch repair genes and InSiGHT
refs: Thompson BA et al. Nat Genet 2014;46:107
text: The International Society for Gastrointestinal Hereditary Tumours (InSiGHT) classified thousands of variants in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 and PMS2, the Lynch syndrome genes, using a standardised scheme that combines clinical data such as tumour microsatellite instability and immunohistochemistry, segregation, functional assays and calibrated in silico priors. Many missense variants in these genes remain of uncertain significance because tumour and family data are needed to resolve them.

title: RASopathy genes
refs: Gelb BD et al. Genet Med 2018;20:1334
text: RASopathies such as Noonan syndrome are caused largely by gain of function missense variants in RAS MAPK pathway genes. The ClinGen RASopathy expert panel adapted the criteria accordingly: PVS1 does not apply because loss of function is not the mechanism, hot spots and functional domains defined by the panel support PM1, de novo occurrence is frequent and well weighted, and very low population frequency thresholds apply. Benign classification relies heavily on population data and segregation.

title: MYH7 and inherited cardiomyopathy
refs: Kelly MA et al. Genet Med 2018;20:351
text: The ClinGen inherited cardiomyopathy expert panel specified the criteria for MYH7, which causes hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathy mainly through missense variants in the myosin head and rod. PVS1 is not used because loss of function is not established; the panel set gene specific allele frequency thresholds that reflect disease prevalence and penetrance, counted probands for PS4, and defined a region of the protein for PM1. Many benign classifications come from frequency evidence.

title: CFTR and the CFTR2 project
refs: Sosnay PR et al. Nat Genet 2013;45:1160
text: Cystic fibrosis is recessive, so a pathogenic CFTR variant need only cause disease in combination with another. The CFTR2 project classifies variants by clinical consequence in patients (sweat chloride, pancreatic status, lung function) together with functional data, distinguishing variants that cause cystic fibrosis, those that do not, and those of varying clinical consequence. p.Phe508del is the most common pathogenic allele. Carrier frequencies are high in some populations, so frequency thresholds for benign evidence must allow for recessive inheritance.

title: Loss of function and gain of function mechanisms
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: The disease mechanism decides which criteria are meaningful. Where haploinsufficiency or biallelic loss causes disease, null variants are strongly informative (PVS1). Where disease results from gain of function or dominant negative effects, truncating variants may be harmless and missense variants in specific regions are the cause; PVS1 is inappropriate and PM1, PS3 and PP2 become more important. Mechanism can be judged from the spectrum of established pathogenic variants and from curated dosage sensitivity.

title: Haploinsufficiency and dosage sensitivity
refs: Riggs ER et al. Genet Med 2020;22:245
text: A gene is haploinsufficient when one working copy is not enough for normal function, so heterozygous loss of function causes disease. ClinGen's dosage sensitivity curation scores haploinsufficiency and triplosensitivity from zero (no evidence) to three (sufficient evidence). Population constraint metrics such as pLI and the loss of function observed over expected ratio indicate intolerance to loss of function but do not by themselves establish a disease mechanism.

title: Gene constraint metrics
refs: Lek M et al. Nature 2016;536:285
Fadista J et al. Bioinformatics 2017;33:471
text: Constraint metrics compare the number of protein truncating or missense variants observed in a large population with the number expected under neutral mutation. The probability of loss of function intolerance (pLI) close to one marks genes depleted of truncating variation. LoFtool ranks genes by intolerance, with low percentiles most intolerant. Constraint describes selection in the general population; recessive disease genes and late onset genes such as BRCA1 can have low pLI despite clear loss of function pathogenicity, so constraint is a feature, not a mechanism.

title: Circularity in computational evidence
refs: Grimm DG et al. Hum Mutat 2015;36:513
text: Predictors trained on public databases can look better than they are because the variants they are tested on, or other variants in the same genes, were in their training data (type one and type two circularity). Grouping cross validation by gene, excluding test variants from all evidence tables, and calibrating on held out predictions reduce the problem. When a predictor uses gene level features its score partly restates gene level evidence such as PP2, which should be kept in mind when both are applied.

title: Splicing variant interpretation
refs: Walker LC et al. Am J Hum Genet 2023;110:1046
text: The ClinGen SVI splicing subgroup recommended a unified approach: use PVS1 for variants at the canonical dinucleotides, PP3 for variants elsewhere predicted to disrupt splicing, BP4 when no splice impact is predicted, and BP7 for synonymous and deep intronic variants without predicted impact. RNA assays observing aberrant splicing can be used in place of predictions, with strength depending on the completeness of the effect. Splice region positions most often affected are the last three exonic bases, positions plus three to plus six of the donor and the polypyrimidine tract and branch region of the acceptor.

title: Deep intronic variants and pseudoexons
refs: Walker LC et al. Am J Hum Genet 2023
text: Most deep intronic variants are benign, but some create a new splice site that activates a pseudoexon and disrupts the transcript. Such variants are rare and usually need RNA evidence. Without a predicted or observed effect, deep intronic variants beyond the splice region can receive BP7; with a prediction of a new splice site they deserve RNA study before any pathogenic evidence is applied.

title: Synonymous variants
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: Synonymous variants do not change the amino acid but can affect splicing, especially near exon boundaries, and occasionally mRNA stability or translation. The majority are benign. A synonymous variant outside the exonic splice region with no predicted splice effect supports a benign interpretation through BP7; one in the last three bases or the first base of an exon needs a splice prediction or RNA evidence.

title: Stop loss variants
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: A stop loss variant removes the termination codon and extends the protein until the next in frame stop in the 3 prime untranslated region, or leads to non stop decay if none is found. It is treated as a protein length change under PM4. The effect depends on the length and nature of the extension and on whether the gene is sensitive to C terminal changes.

title: Untranslated region variants
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: Variants in the 5 prime and 3 prime untranslated regions are mostly benign, but some create upstream open reading frames, disrupt upstream start codons, alter polyadenylation signals or affect regulatory elements. The ACMG/AMP framework offers few criteria for them beyond population and segregation data, so they are often classified as uncertain unless frequency evidence resolves them.

title: Penetrance and age of onset
refs: Whiffin N et al. Genet Med 2017
text: Penetrance is the chance that a carrier develops the disease. Reduced penetrance, common in inherited cancer and cardiomyopathy genes, raises the frequency at which a pathogenic variant can still be found in the population and weakens benign evidence from healthy carriers (BS2) and from frequency (BS1) unless thresholds are adjusted. Late onset means that apparently healthy adults in population databases may still develop disease.

title: Founder variants
refs: Karczewski KJ et al. Nature 2020
text: Founder variants arose in an ancestor of a population that later expanded, so they reach unusually high frequency in that group: BRCA1 c.68_69del and c.5266dup and BRCA2 c.5946del in Ashkenazi Jewish populations are classic examples. Frequency based benign criteria must account for founder effects, which is one reason the filtering frequency calculation usually excludes bottlenecked populations.

title: Copy number variants are out of scope
refs: Riggs ER et al. Genet Med 2020;22:245
text: Deletions and duplications of whole exons, genes or chromosomal regions are classified with a separate ACMG and ClinGen technical standard that scores gene content, dosage sensitivity and case data. Allelion Verdict AI handles sequence variants described in HGVS; intragenic deletions entered as c. descriptions are treated as indels, and whole gene events need the copy number framework.

title: Somatic variants use a different framework
refs: Li MM et al. J Mol Diagn 2017;19:4
text: Somatic variants in tumours are interpreted with the AMP, ASCO and CAP tiers, which grade clinical significance for diagnosis, prognosis and therapy (tiers one to four), not pathogenicity for inherited disease. The germline ACMG/AMP criteria should not be applied to tumour only findings, and a variant can be an actionable somatic driver while being absent from the germline.

title: Mitochondrial DNA variants
refs: McCormick EM et al. Hum Mutat 2020;41:2028
text: Mitochondrial DNA variants need specifications that account for heteroplasmy, maternal inheritance, tissue variability and the absence of standard coding nomenclature for some genes. A ClinGen expert panel published adapted criteria in 2020. The nuclear gene criteria in Allelion Verdict AI do not cover them.

title: Pharmacogenomic and risk alleles
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: Drug response variants (for example in CYP2C9, VKORC1 or DPYD) and low penetrance risk alleles are not pathogenic in the Mendelian sense and are outside the five tier framework. ClinVar records them with separate labels such as drug response, risk factor and association, and the blind evaluation in Allelion Verdict AI excludes them.

title: Secondary findings
refs: Miller DT et al. Genet Med 2021;23:1381
text: ACMG maintains a list of medically actionable genes for which pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants should be reported as secondary findings from exome or genome sequencing, including BRCA1, BRCA2, the mismatch repair genes, several cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia genes and familial hypercholesterolaemia genes. Only pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants are reported as secondary findings; uncertain variants are not.

title: Literature evidence and duplicate probands
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: Case reports are a major source of evidence for PS2, PS4, PM3 and PP1, but the same patient often appears in several papers and database submissions. Curators should check author lists, institutions and patient descriptions before counting probands, prefer primary data over review articles, and record the PubMed identifier of every observation used.

title: Reclassification
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: Classifications change as evidence accumulates. Large studies show that most reclassified uncertain variants move to likely benign or benign, while reclassification of pathogenic variants is uncommon. Laboratories should date every classification, keep the evidence that supported it, and recontact clinicians when a reported classification changes in a way that affects care.

title: Reporting language and limits
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: A variant classification describes the evidence that a variant causes a particular disease. It is not a diagnosis, a risk estimate or a treatment recommendation for an individual, and it should be communicated by qualified professionals together with the clinical context. Allelion Verdict AI drafts evidence summaries for curators and does not give individual medical advice.

title: Missense variants and the residue level view
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: Three criteria look at the variant's neighbourhood in the protein: PS1 for the identical amino acid change from a different nucleotide change, PM5 for a different change at the same residue, and PM1 for clustering of pathogenic variants without benign variation. They use evidence from other variants, so the evidence tables must exclude the variant under review, and they rely on the quality of the classifications used as comparators.

title: Frameshift variants near the 3 prime end
refs: Abou Tayoun AN et al. Hum Mutat 2018
text: Frameshift and nonsense variants close to the end of the coding sequence can escape nonsense mediated decay and produce an almost full length protein. The SVI tree asks whether the truncated region is critical (for example because pathogenic variants are known further downstream) and how much of the protein is removed. A truncation removing a few C terminal residues of a protein without a known C terminal function may receive only moderate PVS1 or none.

title: In frame deletions and insertions
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: In frame deletions and insertions keep the reading frame and remove or add amino acids. In conserved functional regions they support pathogenicity through PM4; in repetitive, low complexity or poorly conserved regions with nearby benign in frame variation they support a benign interpretation through BP3. CFTR p.Phe508del is the best known pathogenic in frame deletion.

title: Allele frequency thresholds for recessive genes
refs: Whiffin N et al. Genet Med 2017
text: For recessive disorders, pathogenic alleles can be carried by healthy heterozygotes at appreciable frequency. The maximum credible allele frequency for a recessive disorder scales with the square root of prevalence, so it is much higher than for a dominant disorder of similar prevalence. PM2 can apply to a recessive variant that is present at a very low frequency, and BS1 thresholds must be set high enough to avoid calling common pathogenic alleles benign.

title: What the blind evaluation measures
refs: Allelion Verdict AI evaluation design
text: Allelion Verdict AI is scored against expert panel and practice guideline classifications in ClinVar, frozen and hashed before any evidence table or model was built. The engine sees only data any curator could gather without case records: population frequency, transcript structure, gene level spectra and allelic evidence from other variants, and calibrated predictors. Expert panels also used case data, functional assays and family studies, so a pathogenic reference variant classified as likely pathogenic or uncertain by the engine usually reflects missing case level evidence rather than an error in the evidence that was available.

title: Choosing a predictor in advance
refs: Pejaver V et al. Am J Hum Genet 2022
text: To avoid cherry picking, ClinGen recommends choosing one calibrated predictor in advance for PP3 and BP4, using it for every variant, and reporting the score with the strength it earns. Running several tools and choosing the most convenient result inflates evidence. Scores in the indeterminate range between the benign and pathogenic thresholds give no computational evidence in either direction.

title: Phenotype ontology and similarity
refs: Gargano MA et al. Nucleic Acids Res 2024
Kohler S et al. Am J Hum Genet 2009;85:457
text: The Human Phenotype Ontology describes clinical abnormalities as terms in a hierarchy and annotates diseases with the terms that characterise them. Semantic similarity measures compare a patient's terms with a disease profile by finding, for each patient term, the most informative shared ancestor in the hierarchy; rare, specific terms count more than general ones. An empirical p value from comparing the same patient terms against many random genes shows whether a match is unusually good.

title: Splice region positions plus three to plus six
refs: Walker LC et al. Am J Hum Genet 2023
text: Outside the invariant dinucleotides, the donor positions plus three to plus six and the acceptor positions minus three to about minus twenty are part of the splice consensus. Changes here, particularly at plus five, frequently weaken splicing. Their pathogenicity is variable and depends on the strength of the native site, so predictions are graded through PP3 rather than PVS1 unless RNA studies show a complete loss of normal splicing.

title: Interpreting the Allelion points bar
refs: Tavtigian SV et al. Hum Mutat 2020
text: The points bar sums every met criterion: pathogenic criteria add and benign criteria subtract. Bands mark the class thresholds (ten for pathogenic, six for likely pathogenic, minus one for likely benign and minus seven for benign). Criteria listed as not evaluated need case level information; adding it in the case evidence panel can move the classification, which shows the curator exactly which missing data would change the outcome.

title: Mosaicism and somatic contamination
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: A variant present in only a fraction of cells, either through post zygotic mutation or clonal haematopoiesis in blood, can appear at a low variant allele fraction. Mosaic de novo variants still count toward PS2 when confirmed, but clonal haematopoiesis can create apparent germline variants in older individuals, particularly in genes such as TP53, so low allele fractions deserve confirmation in another tissue.

title: Variant evidence summary structure
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: A good variant evidence summary states the variant in HGVS on a named transcript, its predicted consequence, population frequency with the database and version, computational evidence with the tool and score, relevant gene level and allelic evidence, case level evidence with identifiers, the criteria applied with strengths, and the final classification with the date. Each statement should be traceable to its source.

title: Limits of a data driven hot spot
refs: Richards S et al. Genet Med 2015
text: Counting classified variants in a window approximates a hot spot but inherits the biases of the database: heavily tested genes and well studied regions accumulate classifications, and recurrent founder variants can inflate counts. Expert panels define hot spots from structural and functional knowledge as well. A data driven PM1 should therefore be read with the counts it rests on and capped together with PP3.

title: Absence from population data and coverage
refs: ClinGen SVI PM2 recommendation 2020
text: A variant can be absent from a population database because nobody carries it or because the site was not sequenced well. Exome datasets cover coding exons and nearby intronic bases; genome datasets cover most of the genome at lower depth. Indels in repetitive sequence are often missed. Absence should be accepted only where coverage is adequate, and the statement should name the database version.

title: Benign evidence from population data
refs: Ghosh R et al. Genet Med 2018
Whiffin N et al. Genet Med 2017
text: Most benign classifications in practice rest on population evidence: a frequency above five percent (BA1), a frequency too high for the disorder (BS1), or observations in healthy individuals inconsistent with a penetrant disorder (BS2). Combined with computational evidence of no effect (BP4) or a synonymous change without splice impact (BP7), they resolve the large majority of common and low frequency variants without any case data.

title: Two ways of combining evidence can disagree
refs: Tavtigian SV et al. Genet Med 2018
text: Because the 2015 rules list fixed combinations, some evidence sets fall between them, and any mixture of pathogenic and benign criteria forces an uncertain call. The point system sums the evidence instead, so weak benign evidence can be outweighed by strong pathogenic evidence. Allelion Verdict AI reports both; the point system is the primary result and the 2015 rules are shown for laboratories that still report with them.

title: Using the evidence copilot
refs: Allelion Verdict AI design
text: The evidence copilot answers questions about criteria, genes, diseases, variants and the literature corpus from a fixed local knowledge base. Every sentence of an answer cites a numbered evidence item and is checked against it before it is shown; sentences that the check cannot support are flagged. It does not give individual medical advice, does not recommend treatment and redacts personal identifiers from questions before anything is logged.
